For the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the recent observed level, expecting minimal movement over such a short window — markets or indices tend to exhibit strong autocorrelation at daily frequencies, so 318.5 represents little more than slight positive drift. For the one-week estimate, I nudged the forecast marginally higher to 319.5, reflecting a small expected trend continuation while acknowledging that weekly moves tend to average out noise. The one-month estimate of 322 extends this gradual drift further, implying roughly a 1% move over the month, which is consistent with moderate historical average returns in many asset classes or index-like series.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval of [311, 326] spans about 15 units, capturing intraday-to-next-day volatility that is relatively constrained. By one week, the interval widens to [305, 334], roughly 29 units, as multiple days of volatility accumulate and the possibility of regime shifts or unexpected data releases grows. The one-month interval of [292, 352] — spanning 60 units — reflects the full breadth of realistic outcomes over four weeks, including the possibility of sustained trending moves in either direction. These widths are roughly consistent with annualized volatility in the 15–20% range for an equity-like series, scaled to each horizon.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst — such as a major policy announcement, stronger-than-expected economic data, or a geopolitical resolution — could drive the series well above 352. On the downside, a sudden risk-off event, financial contagion, or disappointing macro data could break below 292. Liquidity crises or flash crash dynamics are particularly dangerous at short horizons because they can produce large moves in a single session that my one-day interval would fail to capture. Additionally, my estimates assume no structural breaks in the underlying series, so any regime change — a sudden shift in central bank policy or an unexpected geopolitical shock — represents tail risk that is difficult to quantify within standard confidence intervals.
